Antennas and arrays

Analog and digital combining

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows why the position of spatial combining matters to receiver dynamic range.

An analog beamformer combines element voltages before some later receiver stages. A digital beamformer first samples individual channels and then applies complex weights, y = wᴴx. Hybrid systems distribute the combining between analog and digital stages.

Digital weights can form beams and nulls flexibly, but the front ends and ADCs first encounter the uncombined signals. A strong interferer can exceed their linear range before the digital null is formed. Analog suppression placed earlier can reduce that burden, at the cost of hardware and combining constraints.

Powers in dBm must be converted to linear milliwatts before adding. The linear-limit control here illustrates headroom only; it does not model compression, ADC bits, noise figure or a complete multi-element receiver.

Example

A −10 dBm interferer and a −70 dBm desired signal produce a total very close to −10 dBm. If the front-end limit is −20 dBm, the input exceeds it by about 10 dB. A later ideal 40 dB digital null cannot reconstruct samples that clipped earlier.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Why is adding −30 dBm and −30 dBm as −60 dBm incorrect?

    Convert each input to milliwatts before adding.

    Each is 0.001 mW. Their sum is 0.002 mW, or approximately −26.99 dBm.

    2. Where must an interference-reduction stage act if its purpose is to protect a particular amplifier from saturation?

    Follow signal flow toward that amplifier.

    It must reduce the unwanted power before that amplifier. Suppression after the amplifier can improve a later signal statistic but cannot undo the amplifier’s lost linear information.
